To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) we characterized a large number of tick-associated viruses, bacteria, and eukaryotes; 2) we identified pairs of tick microorganisms that were co-infecting ticks more or less frequently than expected; 3) we found pairs of co-infecting micro-organisms whose RNA levels were correlated; and 4) we identified a positive correlation between the RNA levels of South bay virus and the Lyme disease agent, Borrelia burgorferi.
the virome, virobiome and viroeukaryome of the tick Ixodes scapiularis are complex and dynamic, and that some microorganisms co-occur more or less frequently than expected by chance.
we identified a variety of associations between microorganisms in individual I. scapolaris ticks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ecology and evolution of ticks and tickborne pathogens.
understanding the ecology of the tick virosphere and how viruses interact with other microorganisms in ticks.
the ecology of tick-borne microorganisms and how they interact with each other and with the tick host.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the co-infections in ticks are not random, but that they have a specific pattern.
we have identified a number of microorganisms that co-occur or correlate in I. scapolaris ticks and that some of these relationships have the potential to influence the transmission of pathogens.
we found a number of co-occurrence patterns between viruses, bacteria and other microorganisms in I. scapulairis ticks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the I. scapolaris virome is complex and that there is a great deal of variation in the presence and abundance of different viruses in individual ticks.
the tick virome is not just a passive bystander, but rather, tick viruses may be actively interacting with other tick-infecting organisms.

we found evidence of co-infection and associations between viruses, eukaryotes and bacteria in I. scapolaris ticks, and that the two most prevalent viruses were also the ones that had the highest average levels of RNA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is much more to learn about the virome and how viruses interact with other microbes and the tick host.
the tick virome is not simply a passive component of the tick microbiome, but is actively influencing the tick's biology.
tick viromes are not static, but are dynamic, and can change over time and space, and that this dynamic nature can impact tick biology.
